content: We extend our deepest gratitude to the following individuals for their invaluable contributions in providing data related to epidemic thresholds and single-dose antibiotics during the preparation of this guideline: Abdinasi Abubakar from the WHO Country Office in South Sudan. Bradford D. Gessner from Agence de Médecine Préventive, France. Brian Greenwood from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, UK. Chantal Kambire-Diarra from the WHO Country Office in Burkina Faso. Clement Lingani from the WHO Inter-country Support Team for West Africa (IST-WA), Burkina Faso. Daouda Coulibaly from the Ministry of Health, Côte d’Ivoire. Denis Kandolo from the WHO IST-WA, Burkina Faso. Dominique Caugant from the National Institute of Public Health, Oslo, Norway. Emmanuel Musa from the WHO Country Office in Nigeria. Florence Fermon from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), France. Jahangir Houssain from the Meningitis Research Council, Gambia. Jean-Marc Collard from the Institute of Public Health, Belgium. Marc LaForce from the Serum Institute of India, USA. Matthew Coldiron from Epicentre/MSF, France. Rasmata Ouedraogo-Traoré from the Ministry of Health, Burkina Faso. Ryan Novak from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), USA. Sally-Ann Ohene from the WHO Country Office in Ghana. Samba Sow from the Centre pour les Vaccins en Développement, Mali. Sylvestre Tiendrebego from UNICEF/WHO Regional Office, Mali. We also acknowledge the extensive references and research studies that have informed this guideline, including systematic reviews, clinical trials, and epidemiological studies on meningococcal disease, its diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. These references include works published in journals such as The Lancet, BMJ, Clinical Infectious Diseases, and PLOS Medicine, among others. The studies address topics ranging from the economic burden of meningitis, diagnostic accuracy of rapid tests, vaccine effectiveness, and the impact of mass vaccination campaigns on epidemic control. Additionally, the guideline development process was supported by contributions from various WHO regional offices, ministries of health, and international organizations such as UNICEF and Médecins Sans Frontières. The collaborative efforts of these experts and institutions have been instrumental in ensuring the scientific rigor and practical relevance of the recommendations provided. The guideline also incorporates the PICO framework to address critical questions, such as the potential reduction in cases and deaths through mass vaccination campaigns during meningitis outbreaks and the diagnostic accuracy of tests for bacterial meningitis. These questions were systematically evaluated to provide evidence-based recommendations for public health interventions. The development and review of this guideline involved multidisciplinary teams, including the WHO Steering Group, external review groups, and guideline development groups, representing diverse regions and expertise. Their collective efforts have ensured that the guideline is comprehensive, evidence-based, and tailored to address the challenges of meningococcal disease control in various settings.
